artiest/magazine.text:
Magazine was a British rock band, founded in Manchester in 1977 by singer Howard Devoto and guitarist John McGeoch. Devoto had left the punk band Buzzcocks earlier that year because he wanted to make something that went beyond punk. With bassist Barry Adamson, keyboardist Bob Dickinson and drummer Martin Jackson the first line-up took shape; keyboardist Dave Formula soon joined. The band signed to Virgin Records and gave its first concert in Manchester in October 1977.

The first single, Shot by Both Sides, was released in 1978, still with a hard punk sound of guitar, bass and drums. The debut album Real Life (1978) was well received and is regarded as one of the first British post-punk albums. On Secondhand Daylight (1979) the synthesizers took a bigger role, and The Correct Use of Soap (1980) was produced by Martin Hannett. After that McGeoch left for Siouxsie and the Banshees. After Magic, Murder and the Weather (1981) Devoto quit and the band broke up. All four albums reached the British top 40. McGeoch, Adamson and Formula also played in Visage, Steve Strange's group. In 2009 Magazine got back together, and in 2011 No Thyself was released.

Magazine combined the energy of punk with keyboards, unusual chords and Devoto's intelligent, often ironic lyrics. In this way the band was a bridge between punk and the new, more artistic pop music of the 1980s. Simple Minds, The Smiths, Pulp and Radiohead named Magazine as an influence, above all McGeoch's guitar playing.
artiest/magazine.listen: Listen to Shot by Both Sides and notice John McGeoch's sharp guitar and the fast, straight drums, which are still close to punk. Hear how Howard Devoto sings over it, more mocking than angry.

artiest/magdalena-kozena.text:
Magdalena Kožená is a Czech mezzo-soprano, born in Brno in 1973. As a child she sang in the children's and youth choir Kantiléna of the Brno Philharmonic Orchestra. She first wanted to become a concert pianist, but after a hand injury in a sports accident at school she turned to singing. She studied at the Brno conservatory and in Bratislava, won a prize at the International Mozart Competition in 1995 and was attached to the Volksoper in Vienna in 1996 and 1997.

Her first recording was an album of Bach arias, made in the Czech Republic. Deutsche Grammophon then signed her. Italian Cantatas, Love Songs, Juditha triumphans, French Arias, Lamento and an album of works by Dvořák, Janáček and Martinů followed, which won a Gramophone Award in 2001. In 2004 she became Gramophone's Artist of the Year. She often sang with Marc Minkowski, including as Orfeo, Nerone and Mélisande and later in operas by Mozart, among others under Nikolaus Harnoncourt in Salzburg.

Her repertoire runs from the Baroque to the twentieth century. She sings Czech songs and Handel with the same warm, supple voice, and she regularly performs at the Prague Spring festival. In this way she contributes to the classical tradition of Central Europe.
artiest/magdalena-kozena.listen: Listen to a song by Dvořák or Janáček sung by Kožená and notice how she shapes the Czech text into melody. Can you hear how she moves from soft to full singing?

artiest/maggie-nicols.text:
Maggie Nicols is a Scottish singer, dancer and performer in free jazz and improvisation. She was born in Edinburgh in 1948 as Margaret Nicolson. As a teenager she worked as a dancer at the Windmill Theatre, in 1965 she sang for the first time in a club in Manchester and became obsessed with jazz. She sang with the bebop pianist Dennis Rose and in dance bands, and worked for a year as a dancer abroad, including at the Moulin Rouge in Paris.

In 1968 she went to London and joined John Stevens's Spontaneous Music Ensemble. In the early 1970s she gave voice workshops at the Oval House Theatre and played in Centipede, Keith Tippett's fifty-piece big band. With Julie Tippetts, Phil Minton and Brian Eley she formed the vocal quartet Voice. In 1978 she recorded the album Sweet and S'Ours with Julie Tippetts for the label FMP. She became an active feminist and founded the Feminist Improvising Group with Lindsay Cooper. Later she worked with Irene Schweizer and Joëlle Léandre as the trio Les Diaboliques. In 1991 she started a weekly improvisation gathering in London, The Gathering.

She uses her voice as an instrument, with sounds, words and rhythms that arise on the spot. In this way she became an important example for British free improvisation.
artiest/maggie-nicols.listen: Listen to a recording by Maggie Nicols, for example Sweet and S'Ours with Julie Tippetts, and notice how she builds sounds and words without a fixed melody using her voice. Try to hear where she responds to her fellow musician.

artiest/magne-furuholmen.text:
Magne Furuholmen, also known as Mags, is a Norwegian musician and visual artist, born in 1962. He is the keyboardist of a-ha. Around 1980 he played with guitarist Paul Waaktaar-Savoy in the Norwegian band Bridges, which in 1980 released the self-financed album Fakkeltog, with English-language songs. In 1982 the two formed a-ha with the singer Morten Harket.

As early as the age of fifteen Furuholmen came up with the synthesizer riff of Take On Me. According to him, it was Harket who insisted that the band use that riff. Take On Me became a-ha's first and biggest hit, and the song is among the most streamed songs of the twentieth century. With Waaktaar-Savoy, Furuholmen wrote many other a-ha songs, such as Stay on These Roads, Manhattan Skyline, Cry Wolf and Foot of the Mountain. In Manhattan Skyline he wrote the quiet section and Waaktaar-Savoy the rock section. A-ha sold more than fifty million albums. Outside the band Furuholmen made film music with Timbersound and solo albums such as Past Perfect Future Tense (2004) and A Dot of Black in the Blue of Your Bliss (2008).

Furuholmen is also a well-known artist, with exhibitions in Norway, England and elsewhere in Europe, and a large park of ceramic sculptures near Oslo. In 2012 the three members of a-ha were made knights of the Order of St. Olav. Furuholmen shows how in the 1980s the synthesizer could become the melodic heart of a pop song.
artiest/magne-furuholmen.listen: Listen to Take On Me by a-ha and notice the fast, skipping synthesizer riff at the start, which Furuholmen came up with as a teenager. Hear how that riff keeps returning between the verses and how Morten Harket's voice climbs ever higher in the chorus.

artiest/magnus-ostrom.text:
Magnus Öström is a Swedish drummer, born in Skultuna in 1965. He was the child of two artists and grew up with the tastes of his older brother, who listened to Jimi Hendrix, Deep Purple and The Allman Brothers. At eight he built his first drum kit and played with his friend Esbjörn Svensson. He studied at the music academy in Stockholm and played on the Stockholm scene.

To become known he did not have to look far. With Svensson and bassist Dan Berglund he formed the Esbjörn Svensson Trio, e.s.t. for short. That group released twelve albums and toured internationally with great success, until Svensson was killed in an accident in 2008. Öström then took a break. In 2010 he founded his own quartet with guitarist Andreas Hourdakis and two keyboardists. Their first album Thread of Life from 2011 contains a tribute to Svensson, Ballad for E, and won the German Echo Jazz prize in 2012. Searching for Jupiter followed in 2013 with a more optimistic tone. Later releases include Parachute, Taste of Honey and A Room for Travellers.

His playing is shaped by rock, and you can hear that in the groove and the dense sound. Together with e.s.t. he helped bring about a European piano-trio jazz that addressed itself to the rock and pop audience.
artiest/magnus-ostrom.listen: Listen to Ballad for E from Thread of Life and notice how the drums stay soft and restrained and how the atmosphere slowly builds.

artiest/mahalia-jackson.text:
Mahalia Jackson was born in New Orleans in 1911, in a poor family that was still closely tied to the legacy of slavery: both her grandparents had been born into slavery. The church became her home. As a teenager she moved to Chicago, where she sang with the Johnson Singers, one of the first gospel groups. She was not a trained singer. She taught herself everything and drew inspiration from the composer Thomas Dorsey and from the blues singer Bessie Smith, whose way of singing she applied to old Protestant hymns.

Her breakthrough came in the late 1940s with Move On Up a Little Higher. The record sold two million copies and reached number two in the Billboard charts, something never seen before for gospel. She then toured Europe as the first gospel singer to do so, sang for presidents and in 1963 appeared at the March on Washington, as a loyal supporter of Martin Luther King. She turned down offers to record secular music.

She had a powerful contralto and sang with great freedom in melody and rhythm, full of commitment and emotion. Thanks to her success, many other soloists and gospel groups got the chance to perform and record. Pop music also felt her influence: she is seen as an inspiration for the vocal style of rhythm and blues, soul and rock and roll.
artiest/mahalia-jackson.listen: Listen to Move On Up a Little Higher and notice how Jackson keeps stretching and bending the melody a little instead of singing it rigidly. Can you hear how her voice has both power and lightness?

artiest/mahavishnu-orchestra.text:
The Mahavishnu Orchestra was a jazz rock band founded in New York in 1971 by the English guitarist John McLaughlin. McLaughlin had previously played in Miles Davis's band and in drummer Tony Williams's Lifetime. For his own group he chose the Panamanian drummer Billy Cobham, the Irish bassist Rick Laird, the Czech keyboardist Jan Hammer and the American violinist Jerry Goodman. The name came from the Indian guru Sri Chinmoy, whom McLaughlin followed and who gave him the name Mahavishnu.

After a week of rehearsals the band played in the summer of 1971 as the opening act for John Lee Hooker, and a record contract with Columbia soon followed. The debut The Inner Mounting Flame was released in November 1971, Birds of Fire in 1973. The band was famous for its fierce, intricate music and its energetic concerts. Through rapid success, exhaustion and quarrels, the original line-up broke up at the end of 1973. McLaughlin continued with a larger group, with violinist Jean-Luc Ponty and strings, and recorded Apocalypse (1974) with the London Symphony Orchestra, produced by George Martin. From 1984 to 1987 the band existed once more.

The music of the Mahavishnu Orchestra blended jazz, psychedelic rock, funk and Indian classical music, with unusual time signatures and lightning-fast duels between guitar, violin and keyboards. In this way it became one of the most important groups of jazz rock, alongside Return to Forever and Weather Report. Many members later made careers of their own; Jan Hammer, for example, wrote the music for the television series Miami Vice.
artiest/mahavishnu-orchestra.listen: Listen to Meeting of the Spirits from The Inner Mounting Flame and notice how guitar, violin and keyboards play the same fast, intricate melody together. Hear how Billy Cobham's drums beneath it almost never stand still.

artiest/mahmoud-ahmed.text:
Mahmoud Ahmed was born in 1941 in the Mercato district of Addis Ababa. He shined shoes and worked as a handyman at the Arizona Club, the nightspot of the Imperial Bodyguard Band of Emperor Haile Selassie. In 1962 he stepped in when the band's singer failed to show up. After that he remained the regular singer until 1974. In 1971 he recorded his first single and in the 1970s many records and cassettes followed for the labels Amha and Kaifa, with bands such as Dahlak and Ibex.

After the fall of the emperor and under the censorship of the military regime, nightlife disappeared, and from 1978 his work appeared mainly on cassette. He sometimes accompanied himself on the krar, guitar or mandolin. He was one of the first modern Ethiopian musicians to perform in the United States. In 1986 the Belgian label Crammed Discs released the collection Ere Mela Mela, compiled from two Kaifa LPs that he had recorded ten years earlier with the Ibex Band. The world music scene was enthusiastic about it.

His name became internationally greater when the label Buda Musique began the Éthiopiques series in the 1990s. He then toured Europe and America, including with Boston's Either/Orchestra. He is known for tizita, a genre that looks back on the past, slow and grooving, and similar in mood to Portuguese saudade.
artiest/mahmoud-ahmed.listen: Listen to Ere Mela Mela and notice how his voice rises above the band. Can you hear how the rhythm of the accompaniment keeps rolling on while he sings his long, graceful lines?

artiest/mahmoud-guinia.text: Mahmoud Guinia from Essaouira was a maâlem, a master who leads the nocturnal Gnawa ceremony in which music puts the participants into a trance. He played the guembri, a three-stringed bass lute, and sang in a deep, raw voice, accompanied by hand clapping and iron krakebs. In 1994 The Trance of Seven Colors was released, which he recorded with the saxophonist Pharoah Sanders. In this way he became one of the best-known Gnawa voices outside Morocco.
artiest/mahmoud-guinia.listen: Listen to the guembri: one low, humming pattern that keeps coming back, while the krakebs lay a rattling three-against-two rhythm over it.

artiest/major-lazer.text:
Major Lazer is an American dance and DJ group built around the producer Diplo. Diplo and Switch founded the project in 2008, after getting to know each other through their work for M.I.A. In 2011 Switch left. Later Jillionaire and Walshy Fire joined, then Ape Drums, and in 2025 the singer America Foster joined the group. Their music blends reggae, dancehall, reggaeton, soca, house and moombahton.

The debut album Guns Don't Kill People... Lazers Do was released in 2009 and was recorded in Jamaica, at the Tuff Gong Studios. Guest vocalists included Santigold, Vybz Kartel, Mr. Vegas and M.I.A. The first single was Hold the Line. Free the Universe followed in 2013, Peace Is the Mission in 2015 and Music Is the Weapon in 2020, plus EPs such as Apocalypse Soon with Pharrell Williams and Sean Paul and Know No Better with Camila Cabello, Quavo, Travis Scott and J Balvin. Major Lazer also produced Reincarnated, Snoop Dogg's reggae album under the name Snoop Lion. In 2018 Billboard put the group at number five on its Dance 100.

The sound is dance music with a Caribbean soul: heavy bass, dancehall rhythms and many guest vocalists. With tracks such as Lean On, on which MØ sings, Major Lazer made reggae and dancehall part of global electronic pop.
artiest/major-lazer.listen: Listen to Lean On and notice the rhythm that connects Caribbean and electronic sounds, and how MØ's vocals sit above the beat.

artiest/major-lazer-m-en-dj-snake.text:
Lean On was released in March 2015 on the label Mad Decent as the lead single of Peace Is the Mission, Major Lazer's third album. Major Lazer is the project of the producer Diplo. The singer MØ sang the melody, and the French producer DJ Snake contributed to the track. DJ Snake, born William Grigahcine in a Parisian suburb to Algerian parents, had worked his way up from graffiti artist and DJ to producer. He contributed to records by Lady Gaga, among others, and broke through in 2013 with Turn Down for What.

Lean On became an enormous success. The track reached number four in the American Billboard Hot 100 and topped the charts in nine countries. In September 2015 Spotify named it the song of the summer worldwide, and a few months later it was the most streamed title on the service to date. The video, directed by Tim Erem, was shot in India.

The track is an example of how dance music became international in the early 2010s. It blends electronic beats with influences from moombahton and from global club culture, so that it worked both in clubs and on the radio. It shows that a dance hit with its own recognisable sound can at the same time be widely shared.
artiest/major-lazer-m-en-dj-snake.listen: Listen to Lean On and notice the short, high melody that keeps returning, and how the rhythm regains space in the drop after the vocals. Which part stays in your head the longest?

artiest/mal-waldron.text:
Mal Waldron was an American jazz pianist, composer and arranger, born in New York in 1925 to West Indian immigrants. From the age of seven to sixteen he had classical piano lessons, then played saxophone in local bands and, after his army service and a course of study at Queens College, chose the piano for good. Charlie Parker had given him the idea that his own place was not behind the saxophone. From 1950 he played professionally in New York.

In the 1950s he was the pianist of the label Prestige and played on dozens of records, including in groups led by Charles Mingus, Jackie McLean, John Coltrane and Eric Dolphy. For Coltrane he wrote Soul Eyes, his best-known song. From April 1957 until her death in July 1959 he was Billie Holiday's regular accompanist. His own albums from those years are Mal-1, Mal/2, Mal/3 Sounds and The Blues Minus You. In 1963 an overdose cost him his musical ability. He slowly relearned to play, left the United States in the mid-1960s and settled in Europe.

His roots lay in hard bop and post-bop, but he moved towards free jazz. Striking are his tart chords and the repetition of notes and motifs. He recorded more than a hundred albums under his own name and wrote for ballet and film. He died in 2002.
artiest/mal-waldron.listen: Listen to Soul Eyes and notice the calm, almost wistful melody and the tart chords that Waldron places beneath it.

artiest/malachi-favors.text:
Malachi Favors was an American jazz bassist who became known as a member of the Art Ensemble of Chicago. His year of birth is uncertain. Most reference works give 1937, but after his death his daughter said it was 1927. He played mainly double bass, but also bass guitar, banjo, zither, gong and other instruments. At fifteen he started on the double bass and after high school he played professionally. He worked with Dizzy Gillespie and Freddie Hubbard, among others, and in 1959 recorded an LP with the pianist Andrew Hill. Later he added Maghostut to his name.

In 1965 he was a co-founder of the AACM, the Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians in Chicago, and played in Muhal Richard Abrams's Experimental Band. From 1966 he worked with Roscoe Mitchell. From that group the Art Ensemble of Chicago grew. Outside that group he also played with Sunny Murray, Archie Shepp and Dewey Redman. His well-known records include Sightsong, duets with Abrams from 1975, and the solo album Natural & Spiritual from 1978. African Magic in 1979 and The Ritual in 1986 were also released under his name. In 1994 he played with the oud player Roman Bunka and recorded Color Me Cairo.

Favors played in free jazz, but also in bebop and hard bop. He brought a deep, supporting bass sound to a group that also set itself apart with small instruments and theatre. He died in 2004.
artiest/malachi-favors.listen: Listen to a recording by the Art Ensemble of Chicago and notice Favors's double bass, which lays the ground between the horns and the percussion.

artiest/malik-mansurov.text:
Malik Mansurov is an Azerbaijani player of the tar, the long-necked lute that forms the heart of the classical music of Azerbaijan. His albums show where he feels at home. Azerbaïdjan: Chants du Grand Caucase from 2001 presents songs from the Caucasus, The Dastgahs of Azerbaijani Music: The Art of Muqam from 2016 belongs to the great form of the mugham, and Azerbaïdjan: The Tar of Malik Mänsurov puts his instrument at the centre.

The mugham is a classical tradition with long, free improvisations within fixed modes, the dastgahs. A singer and a tar player alternate in long pieces that build up slowly. The tar, with its clear, string-rich sound, provides the melody and the rhythm of the piece.

Nothing was found in our sources about Mansurov's life. The Wikipedia page that went with the name is about Eldar Mansurov, a composer from Baku, and that is a different person. This text therefore stays with what the albums show. The editors still have to add the biography.
artiest/malik-mansurov.listen: Listen to a piece on the tar by Malik Mansurov and notice the clear sound of the instrument. Can you hear how a short melody is played around and slowly expanded?

artiest/malin-broman.text:
Malin Broman is a Swedish violinist, born in 1975. She is concertmaster of the Swedish Radio Symphony Orchestra and plays in the Kungsbacka Piano Trio, the Nash Ensemble in London and the Stockholm Syndrome Ensemble. She is often asked to appear as a soloist and chamber musician. She teaches at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama in London and previously taught at the University of Gothenburg. She is a great-niece of Sten Broman.

Her career began with prizes. In 1994 she won third prize at the Eurovision Young Musicians competition and, that same year, first prize and the audience prize at the Washington International Competition for Strings. In 1996 came second prize at the Carl Nielsen competition in Odense. She has recorded for Hyperion, Alba, BIS and Naxos. During the coronavirus lockdown in 2020 she recorded all eight parts of Mendelssohn's Octet herself. She gave the first performance of Helen Grime's violin concerto and plays a Stradivarius and a viola by Luigi Bajoni, on loan from the Järnåker Foundation. Her albums include Basso Bailando from 2013, Back to StockHome from 2021 and Breaking Waves from 2025.

In 2019 she received the gold medal of the Swedish king for her contribution to musical life. She shows how a classical violinist can carry Swedish musical life and chamber music at the same time.
artiest/malin-broman.listen: Listen to a recording of Broman with the Kungsbacka Piano Trio and notice how the violin converses with the piano and cello instead of merely playing the melody.

artiest/malkit-singh.text:
Malkit Singh is a Punjabi bhangra singer who works in England. He was born around 1963 in Hussainpur, grew up in Nakodar and moved to Birmingham in 1984. There he built a career of more than thirty years and became one of the best-known faces of British bhangra. He was the first Punjabi singer to be awarded an MBE by Queen Elizabeth II, in 2008, and in 2012 he received a star on the Birmingham Walk of Stars.

His best-known song is Tootak Tootak Tootiyan, written by Veer Rahimpuri and released on the album of 1990. That album became at the time the fastest-selling and most successful bhangra album. Other well-known titles are Gur Nalo Ishq Mitha and Jind Mahi. The latter, together with Chal Hun, can be heard in the film Bend It Like Beckham, which meant he was heard outside the Asian community as well. He often appeared on Indian television programmes about Punjabi culture.

Bhangra originally comes from the Punjab and is dance music with a sharp, bouncing rhythm. Singh showed how that tradition acquired a pop form of its own in British cities, with a modern production but the singing and danceability of the Punjabi harvest festivals. In this way he contributes to the story of migrants who took their music with them and made a new popular culture of it.
artiest/malkit-singh.listen: Listen to Tootak Tootak Tootiyan and notice the rhythm that almost forces you to move. Try to hear how vocals and percussion answer one another at the chorus.

artiest/mamie-smith.text:
Mamie Smith was born in 1891 as Mamie Robinson in Cincinnati, Ohio. Around the age of ten she was already touring with a dance troupe, and as a teenager she danced in a travelling show. In 1913 she began singing in the clubs of Harlem in New York. She was a vaudeville singer who mastered various styles, from jazz to blues.

In February 1920 she recorded two songs for the label Okeh. The black songwriter and bandleader Perry Bradford had persuaded the label's boss to record a black singer, despite threats of a boycott. The record sold well. In August 1920 Crazy Blues followed, also written by Bradford. Within a year a million copies had passed over the counter, often bought by African Americans. It was the first recording by a black singer to sing the blues. Record companies then went in search of more black female singers, and sales of so-called race records, records for a black audience, took off.

Smith toured the United States and Europe with her band, the Jazz Hounds. The band included, among others, the young saxophonist Coleman Hawkins. She was billed as the Queen of the Blues, but was soon overshadowed by Bessie Smith. Even so, Mamie Smith opened the door to the classic women's blues of the 1920s. She also appeared in a few films and died in 1946.
artiest/mamie-smith.listen: Listen to Crazy Blues and notice Mamie Smith's powerful, theatrical singing, which sounds more like the vaudeville stage than the raw country blues. Hear how her band's horns play around the vocals.

artiest/man-jumping.text:
Man Jumping was a British group that formed in England in 1983 out of members of the larger collective The Lost Jockey. The group was conceived mainly as a recording project. According to saxophonist Andy Blake, the aim was to develop post-minimalist music further towards rock, funk and dance, without the faults of The Lost Jockey. The line-up consisted of Andy Blake on saxophones and flute, Martin Ditcham on percussion, and Orlando Gough, John Lunn, Glyn Perrin, Charlie Seaward and Schaun Tozer on keyboards, bass and cello.

Their music took ideas from world music, electronics and funk and made of them an alternative world music to dance to. Gough said in 1985 that they came out of systems music and were also influenced by Frank Zappa, James Blood Ulmer and Bach. A demo by the producer Mike Hedges led to a contract with Bill Nelson's Cocteau Records. The first album Jumpcut was released in early 1985 and received enthusiastic reviews. It was chosen record of the year by, among others, The Times, The Guardian and The Independent. In 1987 World Service followed, with Simon Limbrick in place of Ditcham, who had gone on tour with Sade.

The group existed for only four years and two albums, but its influence lasted. Man Jumping connected the mathematical rigour of minimal music with the warmth of dance music, a leap between two worlds that belongs to the pop history of the 1980s.
artiest/man-jumping.listen: Listen to Jumpcut and notice the short, constantly recurring patterns of the keyboards and saxophones. Can you hear how those patterns slowly shift and yet keep a danceable groove?

artiest/man-parrish.text:
Man Parrish grew up in Brooklyn, New York. At fourteen he left his parental home and became a regular at the nightclub Studio 54 in Manhattan. He got his nickname Man from Andy Warhol, and it first appeared in Warhol's magazine Interview. His early performances in hip-hop clubs in the Bronx were spectacles of light, glitter and fireworks, inspired by the atmosphere of Warhol and by groups such as the Cold Crush Brothers.

His first record was Hip Hop, Be Bop (Don't Stop) from 1982. It is electronic dance music with a tight drum machine rhythm and synthesizers: the kind of sound that was called electro in the early 1980s. Parrish said that the record was pulled from the hip-hop scene when it emerged that he was white and gay. His biggest British hit was Male Stripper, made with Man 2 Man, which reached number four.

After his first success he signed with Elektra and got Tony DeFries as his manager, but in 1984 the label dropped him because it did not want to release his finished album. He then mixed and produced for, among others, Boy George, Michael Jackson and Gloria Gaynor. Together with Kraftwerk, Yellow Magic Orchestra and Afrika Bambaataa, he is counted among the makers who shaped electro. In 2018 the Museum of Modern Art in New York added three of his works to its collection, including the video for his debut single.
artiest/man-parrish.listen: Listen to Hip Hop, Be Bop (Don't Stop) and notice the robotic drum machine rhythm and the cool synthesizer sounds. Can you hear how little the track needs to keep you dancing?

artiest/mandy-moore.text:
Mandy Moore is an American singer, songwriter and actress. She was born in Nashua, New Hampshire, in 1984 and grew up in Florida, near Orlando. As a child she wanted to sing and act, and she played leading roles in local productions. At twelve she went to a performing arts summer camp, Stagedoor Manor. Her British grandmother had been a professional ballerina in London, and she found that an inspiration.

In 1999 she broke through with her debut single Candy. The album So Real from the same year was certified platinum. I Wanna Be with You from 2000 became her first single in the American top forty. Mandy Moore in 2001 and Coverage in 2003, an album of covers, followed. With Wild Hope in 2007 and Amanda Leigh in 2009 she moved more towards the singer-songwriter side, later came Silver Landings from 2020 and In Real Life from 2022. Her music began as teen pop and gradually became more grown-up and personal.

At the same time she built a film career, with, among others, A Walk to Remember from 2002 and the voice of Rapunzel in Tangled from 2010. From 2016 to 2022 she played Rebecca Pearson in the series This Is Us. In 2019 she received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. Her career is an example of the teen pop of around 2000.
artiest/mandy-moore.listen: Listen to Candy and notice the light, danceable teen pop sound. Then compare it with a track from Wild Hope and hear how her voice becomes calmer and more personal.

artiest/maneskin.text:
Måneskin is an Italian rock band that formed in Rome in 2016. Singer Damiano David, bassist Victoria De Angelis and guitarist Thomas Raggi knew each other from secondary school; drummer Ethan Torchio joined via an advertisement on Facebook. The name is Danish for moonlight: De Angelis is half Danish, and the others asked her for a few Danish words. The band won a local competition for beginning groups and then played as street musicians in Rome, including on the Via del Corso.

In 2017 Måneskin came second in the Italian version of X Factor. There they played covers such as Beggin' by The Four Seasons and Take Me Out by Franz Ferdinand. The first album Il ballo della vita (2018), with the ballad Torna a casa, went to number 1 in Italy. In 2021 the band won the Sanremo festival with Zitti e buoni, and with it they were able to represent Italy at the Eurovision Song Contest in Rotterdam. They won, as the first rock band since Lordi in 2006. They then broke through all over Europe and America, with Zitti e buoni, I Wanna Be Your Slave and their version of Beggin'. They played as the opening act for The Rolling Stones. Rush! was released in 2023, and since 2024 the band has been on hold.

Måneskin plays hard-hitting guitar rock with influences from glam and hard rock, and the band attracts attention with an exuberant, androgynous image. Their success showed that in the 2020s rock could still reach a large, young audience.
artiest/maneskin.listen: Listen to Zitti e buoni and notice the heavy guitar riff and Victoria De Angelis's tight bass. Hear how Damiano David delivers the Italian lyrics fast and almost rapping, and how the chorus then breaks open.

artiest/manfred-eicher.text:
Manfred Eicher is a German record producer and the founder of ECM Records. He was born in Lindau in 1943 and studied music at the academy in Berlin. At first he was a classical double bassist, later he became a producer. In 1969 he founded ECM, the Edition of Contemporary Music, in Munich.

Many jazz musicians have appeared on the label, among them Paul Bley, Keith Jarrett, Jan Garbarek, Chick Corea, Pat Metheny, Jack DeJohnette and the Art Ensemble of Chicago. Keith Jarrett's The Köln Concert from 1975 became the best-selling solo piano jazz album ever. In 1984 Eicher started the sublabel ECM New Series for classical music, with work by Steve Reich, Arvo Pärt, John Adams, Gavin Bryars, Meredith Monk and the medieval composer Pérotin. Officium from 1994, a meeting between Jan Garbarek and the Hilliard Ensemble, was a great success. Eicher directed the film Holozän in 1992 and wrote the music for the film Kedma in 2002.

Eicher produced most of his label's records himself, more than a thousand albums. A jazz record took on average two days to record and one day to mix, usually with the sound engineer Jan Erik Kongshaug in Oslo. He lets musicians follow their own instinct and himself plays a directing role. The result is a recognisable, spacious and calm ECM sound, which has strongly shaped European jazz. For his work he received, among other honours, DownBeat's Producer of the Year title in 1976 and in 2007 the Bundesverdienstkreuz.
artiest/manfred-eicher.listen: Listen to the beginning of The Köln Concert and notice the space in the recording: how the piano sounds, how quiet it is between the notes and how close the pianist seems.

artiest/manfred-mann.text:
Manfred Mann was a British band that began in London in 1962 and was named after the keyboardist Manfred Mann. The group began as the Mann-Hugg Blues Brothers, with Mann and drummer Mike Hugg, who both came from jazz and knew the London blues wave. By 1963 the line-up was settled, with Mike Vickers, bassist Dave Richmond and the singer and harmonica player Paul Jones. From 1963 the group recorded for His Master's Voice. The first singles did not reach the charts.

The breakthrough came in 1964 with 5-4-3-2-1, the theme tune of the television programme Ready Steady Go!. That same year the band had a number one in England and the United States with Do Wah Diddy Diddy. Pretty Flamingo in 1966 and Mighty Quinn in 1968 again reached number one in England. Paul Jones sang until 1966, then Mike d'Abo. Other members were Tom McGuinness, Jack Bruce and Klaus Voormann. Albums such as The Five Faces of Manfred Mann and Mann Made from 1964 and 1965 show the group in its rhythm and blues period. In 1969 the band broke up. Mann then formed Manfred Mann Chapter Three and in 1971 Manfred Mann's Earth Band.

The group mixed jazz technique with pop, with solos on woodwinds, vibraphone and harmonica. In this way Manfred Mann was an important name in Swinging London.
artiest/manfred-mann.listen: Listen to Do Wah Diddy Diddy and notice Paul Jones's singing, the rhythm and the way the band keeps a simple song tight and playful.

artiest/manfred-schoof.text:
Manfred Schoof is a German jazz trumpeter, born in Magdeburg in 1936. He studied music in Kassel and in Cologne, where the composer Bernd Alois Zimmermann and the big band leader Kurt Edelhagen were among his teachers. He also played flugelhorn and cornet. In the late 1950s and early 1960s he played with the drummer Jaki Liebezeit, the later co-founder of the krautrock band Can.

In the 1960s he started a free jazz group with Alexander von Schlippenbach and Gerd Dudek, which became the basis of the Manfred Schoof Orchestra. His first sextet of his own came in 1965. He sought a blend of composition and improvisation and played with, among others, Albert Mangelsdorff, Peter Brötzmann, Irene Schweizer, Kenny Clarke and the Globe Unity Orchestra. From 1969 to 1971 he played in George Russell's orchestra. Albums from that time are Jazz Meets India from 1967 and European Echoes from 1969. His group took part in performances of Die Soldaten, Zimmermann's opera, and he wrote classical music for the Berliner Philharmoniker. Later came records with Mal Waldron in 1980, Reflections in 1983 and Timebreaker in 1990.

Since 1990 he has been a professor in Cologne and since 2007 chairman of the Union Deutscher Jazzmusiker. Schoof belongs to the first generation of German free jazz, which sought a European sound of its own alongside the American one.
artiest/manfred-schoof.listen: Listen to European Echoes and notice how the horns and percussion play freely around one another and yet follow a shared line.

artiest/manos-hadjidakis.text:
Manos Hadjidakis, also written Hatzidakis, was a Greek composer and thinker about Greek music, born in Xanthi in 1925. His father died in 1931 and his mother took him to Athens, where the family lived in poverty. He studied music theory with Menelaos Pallandios and philosophy at the university, but did not finish that course. He became friends with poets and painters, among them Odysseas Elytis and above all Nikos Gatsos, and took part in the Resistance through the youth organisation EPON, where he got to know Mikis Theodorakis.

His first song was Paper Moon for a Greek staging of A Streetcar Named Desire. In 1947 his piano piece Για μια μικρή λευκή αχιβάδα appeared, and in 1948 he set poems by Gatsos to music. In 1949 he gave a controversial lecture on rembetika, the urban folk music of the Greek port cities. Together with Theodorakis he was one of the founders of éntekhno, in which poets such as Gatsos and folk music come together. In 1960 he won an Oscar for Best Song with Never on Sunday from the film of the same name. He refused the prize because he felt that Athens was wrongly portrayed in the film. He founded the Orchestra of Colours and wrote a great deal for radio and theatre.

His songs connected folk music with Western form and became internationally known. He died in 1994.
artiest/manos-hadjidakis.listen: Listen to Never on Sunday and notice the bouzouki and the danceable Greek rhythm. Can you hear how the song acquires a folk sound without being a traditional song?

artiest/mansour-rahbani.text:
Mansour Rahbani was a Lebanese composer, poet and producer, born in 1925. With his brother Assi he formed the Rahbani Brothers. From 1945 the two worked for Lebanese radio. There they introduced a new kind of song into a world dominated by the traditional Arabic music of the early twentieth century. Later they moved to Near East Radio, where they made a great deal of work, including the sketch series Sabeh and Makhoul.

In 1955 Assi married Nouhad Haddad, better known as the singer Fairuz. With that the group became a trio. The brothers wrote songs and poems, which Fairuz sang with great craftsmanship. They also created a musical theatre of their own, which differs from international opera. In those productions the subject is dignity, truth and great questions about God, man and the country. For film they wrote the music of three films: Biyaa el Khawatem, Safar Barlek and Bent el Hares. Mansour wrote four volumes of poetry. Later came albums such as Saif 840 from 1988, Messe Solennelle from 1995 and The Last Days of Socrates from 2000, the music for a play.

The Rahbani Brothers brought pop songs and theatre together in Arabic, and with Fairuz as the voice their work became known throughout the Arab world. Mansour died in Beirut in 2009.
artiest/mansour-rahbani.listen: Listen to a song by Fairuz that the Rahbani Brothers wrote and notice how her clear voice and the orchestra shape an Arabic melody with an almost cinematic arrangement.

artiest/manu-dibango.text:
Manu Dibango, in full Emmanuel N'Djoké Dibango, was a Cameroonian saxophonist, vibraphonist, bandleader and composer. He was born in Douala in 1933. As a child he learned music in the Protestant church. At fifteen his parents sent him to school in France, where he learned piano and began playing in jazz clubs. In Brussels he met Joseph Kabasele, leader of the Congolese band African Jazz, and in the late 1950s he played with that group in Léopoldville, today's Kinshasa. Kabasele recorded the pan-African anthem Indépendance Cha Cha at that time.

In 1972 Soul Makossa was released. Makossa is an urban dance music from Cameroon, and the word means in Duala roughly: I dance. The track blended jazz, funk and Cameroonian music and was also picked up in America, where in 1974 it received two Grammy nominations. The refrain later became famous through others: Michael Jackson took it over without permission in Wanna Be Startin' Somethin' (1983), and Rihanna used it via Jackson in Don't Stop the Music (2007). Dibango took legal action. Soul Makossa also influenced Jungle Boogie by Kool & the Gang. Later Dibango had a disco hit in England with Big Blow and worked with, among others, Fela Kuti, Herbie Hancock and Sly and Robbie.

Soul Makossa is regarded as the most sampled African song, and Dibango as the most sampled African musician. He brought African music into the discotheques of New York and Paris, long before anyone spoke of world music. He died of COVID-19 in 2020.
artiest/manu-dibango.listen: Listen to Soul Makossa and notice the tight, funky groove of bass and drums, with Dibango's saxophone above it. Listen too for the sung refrain that keeps returning, and then put the ending of Michael Jackson's Wanna Be Startin' Somethin' next to it.

artiest/marc-almond.text:
Marc Almond is an English singer and songwriter, born in Southport in 1957. As a teenager he listened to John Peel on the radio and became a great fan of Marc Bolan, after whom he began to spell his first name, and of David Bowie. Through Bowie he discovered the chansons of Jacques Brel, who became a major influence on him. At the art college in Leeds he made performance art and met fellow student Dave Ball. In 1977 they formed the synthesizer duo Soft Cell together.

In 1981 they recorded Tainted Love, a cover of a northern soul song by Gloria Jones. It became a number 1 hit in England and many other countries, stayed in the American charts for a long time and became one of the defining records of synth-pop. Hits such as Bedsitter, Say Hello, Wave Goodbye and Torch followed, and the albums Non-Stop Erotic Cabaret (1981) and The Art of Falling Apart (1983), recorded in New York. There Almond came into contact with the underground art scene and with Andy Warhol. In 1984 Soft Cell broke up. As a solo artist Almond made albums such as Vermin in Ermine (1984) and Mother Fist and Her Five Daughters (1987), and in 1989 he had a number 1 hit with Gene Pitney with Something's Gotten Hold of My Heart. He also recorded records of songs by Brel and French chansons.

Almond is known for his emotional, soulful voice and his androgynous appearance. He brought cabaret, chanson and torch songs together with electronic pop. In this way he was among the artists who in the 1980s made room for the visibility of gay musicians in pop music.
artiest/marc-almond.listen: Listen to Tainted Love by Soft Cell and notice the bare electronic accompaniment: a synthesizer, a drum machine and two short, dry taps that keep returning. Hear how Almond's voice above it sounds plaintive and theatrical, like an old soul record in a new coat.

artiest/marc-bolan.text:
Marc Bolan, born Mark Feld in 1947 in Hackney in east London, was an English guitarist, singer, songwriter and poet. He was the youngest son of a salesman of beauty products and a woman who ran a stall in the Soho market. In the late 1960s he became known as the founder of Tyrannosaurus Rex, a psychedelic folk group that released four acclaimed albums, with Debora as a minor hit.

Bolan began as an acoustic singer and switched to electric music. The first single of the new group T. Rex, Ride a White Swan, reached number two in England. From 1970 to 1973 T. Rex was as popular in England as The Beatles, with eleven singles in the top ten, four of them at number one: Hot Love, Get It On, Telegram Sam and Metal Guru. The album Electric Warrior from 1971, with only songs by Bolan, became a milestone of glam rock. In March 1971 he appeared with glitter on his face on Top of the Pops with Hot Love, a moment regarded as the beginning of glam rock. From 1973 he mixed rock with funk, soul, gospel, disco and rhythm and blues.

Bolan was killed in a car accident in Barnes in 1977. His influence extends from glam to punk and Britpop. In 2020 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of T. Rex.
artiest/marc-bolan.listen: Listen to Get It On by T. Rex and notice the sharp, raw guitar riff and Bolan's playful singing. Can you hear how simple and danceable rock can be?

artiest/marc-minkowski.text:
Marc Minkowski is a French conductor, born in Paris in 1962. His grandmother was a violinist, his mother is American and his father was the Polish-French paediatrician Alexandre Minkowski. He began as a bassoonist with the Clemencic Consort and the Ricercar Consort. In 1982 he founded Les Musiciens du Louvre, an orchestra for French Baroque music. Among other things it played works by Marin Marais, Jean-Joseph Mouret, Charpentier, Lully and Rameau.

With that orchestra he made many recordings, including Alcyone, Les Amours de Ragonde, Teseo and La Caravane du Caire. He also worked on lesser-known operas by Handel and Gluck. His interest broadened to opera in general. He conducted Mozart's Idomeneo in Paris, Die Entführung aus dem Serail in Salzburg and Giulio Cesare with Cecilia Bartoli, and recorded work by Offenbach. From 2008 to 2012 he was music director of Sinfonia Varsovia, from 2013 to 2017 of the Mozartwoche in Salzburg and from 2016 to 2021 general director of the Opéra national de Bordeaux. In 2026 he was appointed music director of Boston Baroque.

Minkowski brought French Baroque music to wider attention and recorded with singers such as Magdalena Kožená. His conducting style is lively and theatrical, and he showed how little-known work from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries can still captivate.
artiest/marc-minkowski.listen: Listen to a recording by Les Musiciens du Louvre under Minkowski and notice the tight, dancing rhythms of the French Baroque and the clear sound of the period instruments.

artiest/marcel-peres.text:
Marcel Pérès is a French musicologist, composer, choral conductor and singer, and the founder of the early music ensemble Organum. He was born in 1956 in Oran in Algeria, into a family of Spanish descent that returned to France. He grew up in Nice, where he sang in the cathedral and was organist at the Anglican church. He studied organ and composition, followed church music studies in England, worked in Montreal and studied medieval music in France with Michel Huglo.

In 1982 he founded Ensemble Organum, which focuses on what he calls pre- and para-Gregorian chant. The group lived and worked in medieval monasteries, including Sénanque, Royaumont and Moissac. In 1984 he became director of a workshop for research into the performance of medieval music, which later became a European centre. His albums present chants from various traditions, such as Polyphonie aquitaine du XIIe siècle from 1984, Chants de l'Eglise de Rome from 1986, Chants de l'église milanaise from 1989 and Carmina Burana from 1990. He also worked with the Greek singer Lykourgos Angelopoulos on the connection between Western and Byzantine chant. In 1990 he received the Leonardo da Vinci Prize from the Italian government.

Pérès showed how medieval singing can sound like something alive. His own compositions include Le Livre des morts égyptiens from 1979 and Mysteria Apocalypsis.
artiest/marcel-peres.listen: Listen to a recording by Ensemble Organum of Gregorian or Byzantine chant and notice the low, sustained singing and the raw, direct vocal sound, unlike what we are used to from modern choirs.

artiest/marcin-wasilewski.text:
Marcin Wasilewski is a Polish jazz pianist and composer, born in Sławno in 1975. He met the bassist Sławomir Kurkiewicz at the music school in Koszalin and from then on they played jazz together. In 1991 they started a trio of their own. In 1993 the drummer Michał Miskiewicz joined and so the Simple Acoustic Trio was formed, which recorded on small Polish labels.

The trumpeter Tomasz Stańko discovered the young musicians. He took them on tour and in 2001 made the trio his regular band. With him they recorded, among others, Soul of Things in 2001, Suspended Night in 2003 and Lontano in 2005. In 2004 their own career took off, when as the Simple Acoustic Trio they were allowed to record an album for ECM Records. Among others January in 2008, Faithful in 2011 and Spark of Life in 2014, with the saxophonist Joakim Milder, followed. In 2020 Arctic Riff appeared, with Joe Lovano. They also toured as accompanists to Manu Katché.

The trio plays acoustic jazz in the ECM tradition, with a great deal of space, silence and lyricism, a sound that belongs to the European jazz of recent decades. Wasilewski shows that a trio that has played together since youth can make music with almost telepathic insight.
artiest/marcin-wasilewski.listen: Listen to a track from Faithful and notice how piano, bass and drums give one another space. Can you hear how quiet it can be between the notes?

artiest/marcin-wasilewski-trio.text:
The Marcin Wasilewski Trio is a Polish piano trio built around the pianist Marcin Wasilewski, with bassist Slawomir Kurkiewicz and drummer Michal Miskiewicz. The three play together on the German label ECM, which is known for its clear, spacious sound. Their album Trio was recorded in March 2004 and released in April 2005. Among others January (2008), Faithful (2011), Spark of Life (2014), Arctic Riff (2020) and En attendant (2021) followed.

On Trio there is a distinctive mix of original compositions and work by others. The trio plays Björk's Hyperballad, a piece by the Polish composer Karol Szymanowski, Wayne Shorter's Plaza Real and Green Sky by the Polish trumpeter Tomasz Stanko. In this way the three show that pop music, classical music and jazz are not separate worlds for them. Short, freely improvised pieces, such as the Trio Conversation at the beginning and end, are also part of the album.

The American reviewer Thom Jurek called the debut record full of colour, space, drama and beauty. He wrote that the three may not be flashy soloists, but play together so naturally that it sounds astonishing. That is also what makes this group special in Polish jazz: the piano trio works as a single instrument, in which no voice drowns out another.
artiest/marcin-wasilewski-trio.listen: Listen to January and notice how piano, bass and drums play together as equals. Can you hear who takes the lead at which moment, and how much space remains between the notes?

artiest/marco-borsato.text:
Marco Borsato is a Dutch singer, born in Alkmaar in 1966 to an Italian father. After his parents' divorce he lived for a long time in Italy, and he speaks fluent Italian. He was working as a cook when he won Henny Huisman's Soundmixshow in 1990. He then made three Italian-language albums, including Emozioni (1990), which made little impression in the Netherlands.

In 1994, on the advice of his regular songwriter John Ewbank, he began singing in Dutch. His first Dutch-language single, Dromen zijn bedrog, spent twelve weeks at number 1 in the Top 40, then a record, and is still the longest-charting Dutch-language number 1. One hit after another followed. Albums such as Als geen ander (1995), De waarheid (1997) and De bestemming (1998) entered at the top. Between 2003 and 2008 he had nine number 1 singles in a row, something nobody else in the Netherlands managed. In total he scored fifteen number 1 hits in the Top 40, one fewer than The Beatles. He gave series of concerts at De Kuip, the GelreDome and the Sportpaleis in Antwerp. Many of his songs were Dutch versions of Italian songs.

Borsato mainly sang big, emotional ballads about love, farewell and family, with full orchestral arrangements. He became the most successful Dutch artist in the history of the Top 40. From 2021 he was accused of sexual abuse of minors. Radio stations stopped playing his music and his career came to a halt. In December 2025 he was acquitted for lack of evidence.
artiest/marco-borsato.listen: Listen to Dromen zijn bedrog and notice the build-up: the song begins restrained and grows into a big, singalong chorus. Hear how Borsato builds up his voice further and further towards the end.

artiest/marcus-roberts.text:
Marcus Roberts was born in Jacksonville, Florida, in 1963. He has been blind since the age of five because of glaucoma and cataracts. His mother was a gospel singer, his father a dock worker. He learned to play the piano by picking out notes in church, had his first lesson at the age of twelve and went to the Florida School for the Deaf and the Blind, where Ray Charles had also been a pupil. He later studied at Florida State University.

In the 1980s he took the place of pianist Kenny Kirkland in Wynton Marsalis's band. His own records began with The Truth Is Spoken Here (1988) and Deep in the Shed (1990). His music is rooted in the traditional jazz of earlier times. He is influenced more by Jelly Roll Morton and Fats Waller than by McCoy Tyner or Bill Evans, and puts the emphasis on ragtime and stride piano rather than on bebop. In 2009 New Orleans Meets Harlem, Vol. 1 was released, with work by Scott Joplin, Duke Ellington, Morton and Waller.

Roberts also wrote a piano concerto, Spirit of the Blues, commissioned by the Atlanta Symphony Orchestra and the Savannah Music Festival, and appeared as a soloist with symphony orchestras. In 2012 he founded the band The Modern Jazz Generation. He teaches at Florida State University. He belongs to the young generation of jazz musicians who in the 1980s and 1990s made the tradition important again.
artiest/marcus-roberts.listen: Listen to Deep in the Shed and notice Roberts's left hand. Can you hear how it draws its rhythm and chords from old stride piano, while the right hand stays free?

artiest/mari-boine.text:
Mari Boine is a Norwegian Sámi singer, born in 1956 in Gámehisnjárga, a village in Karasjok in the Norwegian county of Finnmark. Her parents were Sámi and made their living from salmon fishing and farming. She grew up in the strict Laestadian church community, where the traditional singing style joik was considered the work of the devil, and at a school where everything was taught in Norwegian. As a young woman she rebelled against the way the Sámi were portrayed in Norway.

Her first records appeared in the 1980s. Her breakthrough was Gula Gula, released in 1989 on her own label Iđut and reissued in 1990 on Peter Gabriel's label RealWorld. Goaskinviellja (1993) and Leahkastin (1994) followed. In 2017 she released See the Woman, her first English-language album. In 1994 Boine refused to perform at the Winter Olympics in Lillehammer, because she saw the invitation as an attempt to display a symbolic minority. In 2008 she became a professor of musicology at Nesna University College.

She sings in North Sámi in a personal adaptation of the joik, accompanied by a mix of percussion and instruments from all kinds of traditions and sometimes rock. Her lyrics deal with discrimination and the beauty of the north, and call for respect for the earth as mother. In this way she became a cultural ambassador of the Sámi.
artiest/mari-boine.listen: Listen to Vuoi Vuoi Mu and notice how her voice moves between singing and joik. Which instruments do you hear beneath it, and do they sound Scandinavian or rather from far away?

artiest/maria-callas.text:
Maria Callas was born in New York in 1923 to Greek immigrants. At the age of thirteen she received her musical training in Greece and later built her career in Italy. She was a soprano and sang a large repertoire, from the bel canto of Donizetti, Bellini and Rossini to Verdi and Puccini, and at the start of her career Wagner too. The press called her La Divina, the divine.

On records from the 1950s her role as an innovator can be heard: I puritani, La Gioconda and Lucia di Lammermoor in 1953, Cavalleria rusticana and Norma in 1954, and Callas at La Scala in 1955. Critics praised her technique, her wide vocal range and her acting. She was almost blind on stage because of her poor eyesight. After a considerable weight loss she developed vocal problems, and her career ended early. Her life was extensively covered by the press, including the supposed rivalry with Renata Tebaldi and her love for the shipowner Aristotle Onassis.

Yet it was first and foremost about her art. Leonard Bernstein called her the bible of opera, and in 2006 Opera News wrote that she was still the definition of the diva as artist. She died in 1977; her ashes were scattered two years later over the Aegean Sea.
artiest/maria-callas.listen: Listen to Carmen: L'amour est un oiseau rebelle (Habanera) and notice how Callas colours every phrase. Can you hear how she plays with tempo and tone, so that the Habanera sounds not only beautiful but also dangerous?
